en: The *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Boy Suvarṇaprabha*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mingjiao Dashi, recipient of the purple robe,
at the Mi-lin Monastery in the kingdom of Jālandhara, Central India.
Translated by the śramaṇa subject Tianxi'ai by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One dressed himself and, surrounded by a respectful retinue of bhikṣus, entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in due order.
A certain brāhmaṇa came out from Śrāvastī and encountered the World-Honored One; gazing long at his dignified bearing, he spoke these words in praise:
"Gautama!..."
"Your face is most excellent, golden and majestic," the World-Honored One confirmed, saying: "So it is!"
"It is so! It is through the merit I have performed that I have obtained this reward.
The Brahmin said:

"Gautama! Even in this present life, I possess merit; for a boy has been born in my home, golden-hued and radiant, with a countenance and features so excellent that he resembles you, Gautama—a marvel never before seen."
"Furthermore, Gautama!
At the time when the youth was first born, there were yet other most wondrous and auspicious events:

at the moment of his birth, his mind was peaceful and serene, and his consciousnesses were clear and sharp; suddenly, lotus flowers sprang up within his courtyard, and a celestial fragrance filled the chamber, remaining perpetually fragrant, such that all sentient beings universally felt love and joy."
"Furthermore, Gautama!
This is neither extraordinary nor rare.
Furthermore, at the time of the boy's initial birth, *campaka* trees sprang up everywhere, those trees bearing exquisite *campaka* flowers of celestial purple-gold color."
"Furthermore, Gautama!
These extraordinary omens are not yet rare.

Moreover, at the time of the boy’s initial birth, celestial golden platters appeared spontaneously; filled within those platters were hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial food and drink, such that even if one were to eat from them, they would never be exhausted."
"Furthermore, Gautama!
Such a response is not yet particularly marvelous.

At the time when the boy was first born, a voice issued from his mouth, saying: 'There shall appear in the world Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and Arhats, and so forth, up to: "I shall always keep them in my thoughts while walking and staying. "
After the brahmin had finished recounting these auspicious matters concerning the boy, he said to the Buddha,
"Please go to that place to see the boy.
The World-Honored One went silently to that house.
As they were about to enter, an upāsaka standing in the middle addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do not enter this house!
That brāhmaṇa has no faith or reverence for the Buddha-dharma."
The World-Honored One replied,
"This brāhmaṇa also possesses the faculty of faith.
Having thus answered the upāsaka, the World-Honored One then entered the brāhmaṇa’s house and saw his young son.

At that time, as soon as the youth saw the World-Honored One, he went to take refuge and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. The Buddha then offered a blessing. In this manner, those bhikṣus followed the Buddha and also saw the youth. After the Buddha had offered the blessing, he returned to the vihāra together with the bhikṣus.

At that time, as the youth gradually grew up, King Prasenajit, the ruler of Śrāvastī, heard that the brahmin possessed such virtuous conduct and had fathered a noble son. He then dispatched an envoy carrying a profusion of flower garlands, sandalwood, and precious incense to the brahmin’s house, where he surrounded the youth and extended an invitation.
The youth replied,
"I shall wait until I have first gone to the Jeta Grove to pay my respects to the World-Honored One, and then enter Śrāvastī to see King Prasenajit.
After the envoy had returned and reported these matters in full, King Prasenajit heard his report.
"I shall now also go to the Jeta Grove to pay my respects to the World-Honored One and see that youth.
At that time, the youth proceeded toward the Jeta Grove, and on the way he encountered a brahmin who asked him,
"Where are you going now?"
The youth replied,
"I wish to go to Jeta’s Grove to pay my respects to the World-Honored One.
The brāhmaṇa rebuked the youth:
“How is it that one born into the noble lineage of the Brahmins must go away to see a śramaṇa?
The youth replied,
“It is as if you had found a great treasure trove of precious jewels, yet did not wish to take those jewels back home.”
"You have come before me in auspiciousness, yet you strike me back with a staff and drive me away.
Having spoken thus to the youth, he proceeded to the Jeta Grove.
Upon arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat before him to listen to the Dharma.
A magnificent lotus flower from the Heaven of Delighting in Births was born within that Jeta Grove; its fragrance was so pervasive that it filled all places, and wisdom suddenly arose in him:
"I shall now take this lotus flower to make an offering to the World-Honored One."
He further reflected:
"When I was first born, the *campaka* tree was a rarity in the world.
At the moment he resolved his mind, a *campaka* tree spontaneously appeared, its branches bearing *campaka* flowers the color of celestial purple gold.
Immediately, the youth cupped campaka flowers in his hands and scattered them over the World-Honored One; the scattered flowers remained upon the Buddha’s body, adorning it.
Among them, some abide upon the Buddha’s crown, some abide within the Buddha’s breast, and some abide beneath the Buddha’s feet;
some form flower garlands and robes, making various offerings such as these.
At that time, the king was struck with wonder and asked the youth,
"How did you perform such a display of supernatural power through your offerings?
The youth replied:
"I have created all such adornments in the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the youth again gave rise to supreme wisdom:

"From my *campaka* tree, following the arising of my thought, *campaka* flowers have blossomed; those flowers grow either on the trunk of the tree, or upon its fruit, or on its branches, or upon its leaves."
Furthermore, *campaka* flowers appeared and remained suspended in the midst of the sky.
Moreover, within the sky above Jetavana, all manner of golden jewel-bells appeared.
At that time, the youth prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and said:
"World-Honored One!
Please accept today’s meal offered by me to the World-Honored One, as well as for all the bhikṣus, the king, and the attendants, so that they may all receive my offerings."
The World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When the time for striking the *ghanṭā* arrived, the World-Honored One sat down with composed dignity, followed by the bhikṣus, the king, and his retinue, who sat down in succession.
At that time, he gave rise to a most supreme and subtle wisdom-thought, reflecting:
"In my previous birth, a golden platter appeared, filled with celestial food.
May it now manifest before me, so that I may bring it to make an offering to the Buddha."
Having formed this thought, a golden platter from his previous life appeared before him according to his wish, filled with the finest celestial flavors.
At that moment, the youth took the golden platter and the food and drink, personally making the offering.

At that time, after the World-Honored One, the bhikṣus, the king, and his attendants had finished eating and were fully satiated, the youth Suvarṇaprabhāsa was filled with great joy. He prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, saying:

"From this point forward, may my roots of goodness increase; having truly resolved upon this vow, I shall extensively practice the Dharma and provide relief to deliver sentient beings. Only thereafter will I attain Buddhahood, providing deliverance for those not yet delivered, bestowing peace upon those not yet at peace, and bringing all who have not attained tranquility to a state of perfect stillness."
At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the youth’s resolve, spoke in succession regarding the characteristics of the hells:

“Namely, the Avīci Hell, the Arbuda Hell, the Nirarbuda Hell, the Aṭaṭa, the Hahava, the Huhuva, the Blue Lotus, the Red Lotus, and the Great Red Lotus; having emerged from these, one enters the eight hot hells.”
"This sequence is entirely caused by the retribution of delusions and karma; if there is one who possesses wisdom and preaches the Dharma of my salvation, they shall attain coolness.
At that time, as the World-Honored One spoke these words, four-colored rays of light—blue, yellow, red, and white—issued forth from his mouth.

Among those rays of light, some ascended into the air, while others descended into the hells, illuminating the Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci hells, as well as the Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma hells.
If they go to the Hot Hells, they obtain coolness; if they enter the Cold Ice Hells, they obtain warmth. Then those sentient beings give rise to a superior thought:
"How may we come to this place?"
"Thus they pass away at the end of their lives and are reborn in other realms.
Once he had formed this thought, the World-Honored One manifested transformative light and dispatched emanations so that he might see them.
Having seen this, they thought:
"After we pass away from this life, we shall certainly not be reborn in any other evil realms.

We have never before seen sentient beings in this place receiving [the fruits of their deeds]; now, having gained faith through this supreme light of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), our karmic debts for the hells are exhausted, and each of us shall be born among humans or in the heavens, truly receiving [the results]."

If this light shines upon those realms above—the Cāturmahārājakāyika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha heavens—once the light has reached them, it utters such sounds, proclaiming suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and recites two verses:
"Daikō exhorts you: take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
shake off the army of the Lord of Death, as an elephant breaks free from its bonds.
If you enter into this Dharma, practice with a sincere heart and do not regress."
"Therefore, the cycle of saṃsāra is severed, and all sufferings are completely exhausted.
At that time, the light shone throughout the trichiliocosm to deliver sentient beings; this light then returned to the Buddha’s body and followed behind the World-Honored One.
At that time, when the World-Honored One wished to bestow a prediction regarding past karma, the light he emitted entered behind his back;
when he wished to bestow a prediction regarding future karma, the light entered before him;
and when he wished to bestow a prediction for those born in hell, the light entered from beneath his feet.
If one is to receive the prediction of rebirth among animals, the light enters through the Buddha’s heel;
if one is to receive the prediction of rebirth among hungry ghosts, the light enters through the Buddha’s big toe;
if one is to receive the prediction of rebirth among human beings, the light enters through below the Buddha’s knee.
If one is to receive the prediction of becoming a Wheel-Turning King of Power (*balacakravartin*), the light enters through the palm of the Buddha’s left hand;
if one is to receive the prediction of becoming a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), the light enters through the palm of the Buddha’s right hand;
if one is to receive the prediction of being reborn in heaven, the light enters through the Buddha’s navel.
If those destined for the enlightenment of a śrāvaka are to receive their prediction, the light enters through the Buddha’s chest;
if those destined for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha are to receive their prediction, the light enters through the Buddha’s ūrṇā between the eyebrows;
and if those destined for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are to receive their prediction, the light enters through the crown of the Buddha’s head.
At that time, the light emitted by the World-Honored One circled his body three times and entered the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
Then, Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of various colors, they issued from his mouth and pervaded the ten directions, illuminating them all universally.
He then spoke in verse:
"This is not for long; it is far removed. All afflictions have been cast away."
The Buddha is supreme in the world; the reward for excellent causes is never in vain.
White as a conch shell or a lotus flower, the Buddha manifests light to subdue Māra;
at that moment, Māra departs of his own accord, and wondrous wisdom is established in tranquility.
Causing the śrāvakas to seek Buddhahood, with the stable and peaceful voice of a Muni,
like the most supreme bull-king, he purifies them by removing the net of all doubts;
free from the bonds of enemies, like water dissolving salt.
“The Perfectly Awakened One has proclaimed the manifestation of light; whom does the Buddha grant the prediction of enlightenment?
Hearing this, they attain the joy of meditative concentration, and this multitude rejoices.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! So it is, Ānanda!"
"It is not that there is no cause and effect, Ānanda!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, speaks correctly."

Ānanda! Behold this youth who has made such offerings to me; his roots of goodness are firm and deep. Having resolved to bestow the Dharma, he will, throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, practice for the sake of bodhi and accomplish the six pāramitās of great compassion. When his contemplative practices are perfected, he will attain equal and right enlightenment, becoming known as the Tathāgata Suvarṇaprabhāsa. He will be fully endowed with the ten powers, possess the perfect clarity of the four wisdoms, and be equipped with the three secrets, the unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion.
"If we had awakened the aspiration for enlightenment in the past, we too would have practiced this gift of Dharma.
At that time, King Prasenajit asked:
"World-Honored One!"
“What kind of karmic actions did this boy perform to attain such wealth and nobility?
The World-Honored One replied, “In his past lives long ago, this boy extensively cultivated the causes of meritorious deeds; it is for these that he has now obtained this retribution.”
Furthermore, when this youth previously sowed the causes of his karma, his resolute mind did not waver; who in this world can escape such retribution?
Great King!
When the karma one has created reaches the time for its fruit to be received, it is as inexhaustible as the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element:
Thus, regarding these aggregates, elements, and six sense objects, the performance of actions and the attainment of their retributions are without end.
Child, because you have planted roots of merit with a sincere mind in the past, you now receive this inexhaustible reward;
even for good and evil karma, the retribution for such deeds is inexhaustible, and even if one were to pass through a hundred kalpas, when the karma arrives, its retribution must be experienced.
"Great King!
In a past age, there was a king in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Śrutisena. He had a crown prince named Śrīguhya.

At that time, the father-king extensively committed sinful deeds; seeing his father committing such sins, the prince’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end, and he addressed the king, saying:"
"I am going to practice the path.
The king said, "You are my only son; how can I now instruct you to go and practice?"
The Auspicious One spoke these secret words:
"I must depart from my father; I shall certainly go forth to practice.
Thus spoke the youth.
"Regarding gold, silver, elephants, horses, palace attendants, and treasuries, his mind was free from greedy attachment and he had no desire for their enjoyment.

Thereafter, he practiced the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and attained the realization of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*). Countless hundreds of thousands of devas and humans came to make offerings to him.
Others, having seen this, informed the king in full:
"The Prince has attained such merit as this.
When the king heard this, he wished to see his son and departed from the palace, followed by the fourfold army.

There was a poor man who saw the king seated upon the back of a supreme elephant, adorned with exquisite garments and fine perfumes smeared upon his body, shaded by a parasol, and surrounded by the fourfold army. He conceived this wisdom:
"This king’s hands, feet, belly, head, face, shoulders, and back are no different from my own; for what reason does he sit upon this supreme elephant?"
Adorned with exquisite garments and fine ornaments, my body anointed with sublime perfumes, a parasol held over me and the fourfold army surrounding me?

Furthermore, throughout successive lifetimes, my body has been burdened by stinginess and greed, never having practiced giving; this has caused me to undergo such suffering in this present life. Since I am so destitute and unable to practice giving, how could I be reborn among those people?
He asked the king again,
"I do not know where Your Majesty has gone.
Upon hearing the words of the army commander, he replied:
"I have a son named Śrīguhya who went forth to practice and realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; if anyone makes even a small offering to him, they will later obtain a great fruit."
Having answered the king's question, the king continued on his way.
At that moment, the king suddenly saw a herd of deer; out of affection for them, he pursued them.
Then the poor man reflected deeply:
"The king is greedily chasing the deer; at this time, I wish to see an *pratyekabuddha*.

Then the poor man gradually moved forward, entered the mountain valley, and beheld that *pratyekabuddha*. His physical stature was majestic and his mind was tranquil; he was surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of worthies and sages, with *mandārava* flowers scattered about piled up to the knees.
At that time, the poor man wailed aloud, filled with profound grief and deep distress.
Meanwhile, after the hundreds of thousands of worthies and sages had finished their offerings, they departed once more.
The poor man realized:
"With what shall I now make an offering to the Pratyekabuddha?
Not far from here there is a mango tree."
At that time, the poor man took the finest *āmra* fruits and filled his bowl to the brim as an offering to the pratyekabuddha.

Then, the pratyekabuddha took the bowl and, like a king of geese soaring freely through the air, manifested various supernatural transformations; he then descended from the sky and returned to his original seat.
Furthermore, the poor man prostrated at the feet of the Pratyekabuddha and said, "Please eat for me;
I shall thereby receive merit. On the second day, he made an offering, and the Pratyekabuddha:
"This man’s mind is pure and awakened," [he thought].
He rescued the poor man and accepted his offerings.
Immediately, the poor man emerged from the mountain valley.
When King Sena heard that the Pratyekabuddha was seen from afar dwelling in the midst of space, wisdom arose within him and he reflected:
"There must be a person of great merit, a human or a deva, at that place; I shall now go quickly to see both the Pratyekabuddha and that person."
The king then entered the mountain valley, and along the way he saw that poor man emerging from the valley.
The king asked him,
"Where have you come from?"
The poor man replied,
"I have come from this place.
The king said:
“O poor man!
Your body is coarse and rough, your hair is disheveled, and your clothes are soiled and unwashed; how can you now distance yourself from poverty and become as wealthy and noble as I?”
"I observe that you truly cannot escape poverty.
After the man had taken his leave of the king, he suddenly reflected:
"How can I obtain a single plot of excellent land?"
"And how did you obtain such various exquisite foods, complete with a hundred flavors?
Before he had finished reflecting, his foot stepped upon a round stone and he suddenly fell to the ground; there, at that spot, he found an iron jar filled with gold and jewels.
When the king reached the mountain, he saw that pratyekabuddha and sat before him.
After staying for a short while, he addressed his son, saying:
"I have come to offer prayers; how about you accept my meal offering tomorrow?"
The Pratyekabuddha replied,
"Great King!
I have already accepted an invitation."
Upon hearing the general’s question,
“At whose invitation have you come?
the Pratyekabuddha replied:
"A poor man has invited me for a meal offering.
The King then dispatched a messenger to tell the poor man:
"I have invited a Pratyekabuddha for a meal; you may invite him on another day."
When the envoy arrived, he delivered the king’s decree in full.
The poor man refused; thereupon the king went in person to the poor man’s dwelling and spoke again:
“I shall provide food for the pratyekabuddha, while you may prepare the meal on another day.”
He replied, "I cannot.
The king said,
"You must change the date."
The poor man said:
"How can you ask me to postpone the day?
Moreover, I possess my own gold and jewels with which I shall certainly extend my offerings."
The king said:
"You were originally poor, whereas I am of the Kṣatriya lineage of consecrated kings; how then can you say that you have gold in my presence?"
The poor man said, "If Your Majesty does not believe me, I shall show you the gold.

He then went with him to the place where the gold was extracted; there stood an iron vat from which gold and jewels were poured out, heaped up like a mountain, such that if one person stood on one side, they could not see those on the other side.
The king then reflected:
"Does this person possess such merit and virtue?
That person replied:
"The time for my fast has arrived.

On the second day, the poor man cleared the field, adorned it most exquisitely, scattered various lotus flowers, fashioned wonderful parasols from tree branches and leaves, and prepared a meal as an offering.
Then that Pratyekabuddha ascended further into the air and manifested various supernatural transformations.
At that time, the man prostrated at his feet and made this vow:
"Just as these flowers have been scattered upon this ground to become lotuses, may I, in every life and birth throughout all my existences, obtain those wondrous celestial lotuses."

Just as I have made this offering of a tree-branch parasol, may I, by virtue of this virtuous vow, obtain *campaka* trees in every life and every birth, from which bloom *campaka* flowers the color of celestial purple gold;

and just as I have offered food in an earthenware vessel, by the root of this merit, may I always obtain golden plates filled with celestial food in every life and every birth, such that even if hundreds or thousands of people were to eat, it would never be exhausted, and may I encounter a Buddha.
He addressed King Prasenajit:
"You must reflect upon this!
That poor man at that time was none other than the present Brahmin youth, Suvarṇaprabha."
"By making offerings to those who have attained enlightenment, one's roots of goodness will become boundless in their joy, and all aspirations of the heart shall be fulfilled.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, those bhikṣus received it with single-minded devotion and joyfully put it into practice.
The Sūtra on the Youth Suvarṇaprabhāsa Spoken by the Buddha.
